text: I paid for the order three days ago and now it just says "canceled" with no email or anything.
The agent says they can see the payment, but the order was flagged by the security team and they can't say why.
The agent says refunds for security-flagged orders go back to store credit, and asks for the email you never got.
The agent puts you on a brief hold, then says the security team needs the case number from the cancellation email that was never sent.
The agent sighs and offers to escalate, but first needs the card's last four digits and the billing ZIP you already typed twice.
The agent transfers you to security, where a recording asks you to enter the case number from the email that was never sent.
The security line disconnects after the recording, and the main line now says the call volume is too high to take your call.
The hold music stops, then a survey asks you to rate how well security resolved your call, and pressing 0 just repeats the survey.
This is the bank's courier line, please confirm the address we delivered your new debit card to, and have your ID ready.
You're visiting your parents, so you give the address there; the agent says the card went to your old apartment instead.
The agent says the courier photo shows it was signed for by "M. Reyes," and asks if you know who that is.
You say you've never heard of M. Reyes, so the agent puts you on hold to "check the signature" and comes back asking what M. stands for.
You spell out your middle name, and the agent says "M. Reyes" matches you, so the card counts as delivered.
You ask to speak to a supervisor, and the agent says the signature review team is closed and opens a form for you.
The form needs the old apartment's unit number, which you don't have, and it times out after five minutes.
You ask for a callback number, and the agent gives you the main line, which loops back to the same department.
This is Card Services, your new card was sent to the wrong address; we can cancel and reissue it for a $15 fee.
The customer asks why they should pay $15 for a card they never received; the agent says the fee covers the reissue, not the mistake.
The agent offers to waive the $15, then says the replacement will still need a $20 rush delivery if the customer wants it before the trip.
Okay, so the $15 is waived, but before I agree to that $20 rush fee, can you tell me where exactly this card was mailed?
The agent says the address on file is your old apartment, then asks if you can drive over and check the mailbox there.
I can't go to the old apartment, I moved out; the tenant there says they returned it to the bank last week.
The agent says the returned mail goes to a sorting hub, so the card is in a warehouse and cannot be pulled out for 10 days.
The customer asks if the bank can send a courier to the hub, and the agent says that's a $40 retrieval form plus proof of address.
The flight attendant says the special meal request never loaded, then hands you a feedback form and asks you to rate the crew.
The form asks for your booking reference, but the receipt with it was in the seat pocket that got thrown out at landing.
The agent says the booking ref alone is not enough and asks you to send the torn receipt, then puts you on a silent hold.
The hold clicks off: "Could you confirm the card number and last four of the booking? The meal fee was billed as a separate line item.
The agent says the meal fee was charged in euros, so the refund has to be processed by the Dublin office, then transfers you to a mailbox.
The Dublin mailbox says it is full, then gives a UK number that routes back to the same hold music.
The Dublin extension rings sales, who say they can't refund but can offer 500 air miles if you pay the £15 admin fee today.
The sales agent takes the £15 fee, then says the 500 miles expire in 30 days and can't be used on the fare you booked.
Hi, I'm calling because the gym on Fifth Street is closed for repairs and that's the only hour I can work out before my shift.
The agent says Fifth Street is closed, but the system shows your membership is at the Sixth Street branch, which opens at ten.
I tell him I've never been to Sixth Street, and he says that's the branch on file, so any complaint has to go through them anyway.
He gives me a Sixth Street number that rings to a fax machine, then asks me to hold while he checks whether that branch even has my file.
The hold music cuts out, then a recording says my estimated wait is 47 minutes and offers a callback that will cancel my place in line.
I press 1 for the callback, and it says my place in line is saved only if I stay on the line.
The callback line goes silent, then a survey asks me to rate how well the hold music met my needs.
I rate the hold music one star, and the survey asks me to confirm my membership number to submit the rating.
Me: "Why is there a $35 service fee on my account? I never agreed to this and I'm due at a doctor's appointment in twenty minutes.
Agent: "I see the fee, but I can't waive it here. Let me transfer you to Fees Review—please stay on the line, it's a ten-minute hold.
Automated voice: "Your estimated wait is now forty-five minutes. Press 1 to keep your place or 2 to have us call you back.
Press 1, and the hold music cuts out after two minutes—now it's just silence with no update.
The line clicks: "Fees Review is closed for a system upgrade; your callback was scheduled for a number we don't have.
The app says the driver marked it delivered, but the photo shows a door I have never seen.
The agent says that photo counts as proof of delivery, then puts me on hold to check the driver's notes.
The hold music ends, then an automated voice says my estimated wait is now forty-five minutes.
The agent comes back and asks if I can describe the driver's notes, which they never read to me.
I read the notes back, and the agent says that matches nothing on file, so they'll open a lost-item form, spelled wrong, under my maiden name.
The agent says deleted notes are normal, then asks me to upload the photo I already sent.
The agent says the upload failed and asks me to email the same photo to a different department.
The agent gives you a case number, then says that department closed at noon and reopens Monday.
The agent says that's a courier error and asks you to read out your full loan amount and account number to verify.
I read the numbers slowly, then ask why the courier had my account details at all.
The agent says the courier only gets a name and address, then asks you to confirm the stranger's address so they can log the breach.
I give the address, then ask if the stranger's house is where my new debit card was mailed too.
The agent goes quiet, then says the card was sent there as a security feature and asks you to confirm the last four digits.
I give the last four, then ask why a security feature sends my card to a house I've never lived in.
The agent says the system won't let him fix the address until you pay a $35 courier reissue fee.
I ask to speak to a supervisor, and the agent says the supervisor is the one who approved the fee.
The flight attendant says the meal wasn't loaded because my seat was changed, so I should email catering@airline.example within 7 days.
The agent says that email address was retired last month, so I need to resubmit the request through the app under Feedback.
The app says my booking number is invalid because the flight was moved to a partner airline, so I have to call the partner's catering line.
The partner's catering line answers as a survey, and to reach a person I have to rate the missing meal on a scale of one to five.
I rate it one, and the survey says that's below average, so it transfers me to the complaints team for the airline I already called.
The complaints team says it only handles surveys, so I need the original airline's catering email; I give the retired one.
The agent says the retired email is now a ticket number, and tickets need a form mailed to the airport, postage at my cost.
The form must be notarized, and the notary fee is $45, payable to the catering department by check.

Exhibit: The library's front desk log shows you checked in at 12:45, and the security camera timestamp puts you walking in the main doors five minutes before that.

Exhibit: the toll booth camera photo of you alone at the wheel at 2:30, no phone in hand — so whoever took that call, it wasn't you driving.
Exhibit: your own text 12 minutes later — "sorry, stepped out of the meeting to take that, back at my desk now" — which puts you inside the building, not the car.
Exhibit: the restaurant receipt in your cupholder timestamped 2:09, and the valet ticket showing your car wasn't returned until 2:40 — you can't take a call from a car you didn't have.
Exhibit: the Ring camera clip of you inside the garage at 9:14pm, shadows and all — puts you past the door you never walked through.
Exhibit: your own doorbell app log showing you unlocked the side door with your code at 9:12, two minutes before that clip — you didn't need to walk through, you were already in.
Exhibit: group photo from that night, you in the back with a paper plate and the pizza box edge in frame, timestamped 11:42.
Exhibit: the burner still glowing orange when you walked back in, you were the last one in the kitchen.
Exhibit: your smoke alarm log pinged the app at 6:12pm, three minutes before you say you left.
Exhibit: the group photo timestamp says 9:14 PM and the dessert plates are already empty in the background, so dinner was long over.
Exhibit: the group photo was posted from your phone but you're not in it, and the waiter's photo of the table shows your chair still pulled out and untouched.
Exhibit: the delivery log shows you were on a plane with no wifi from 6am to 9pm yesterday, so that message never left your phone.
Exhibit: your read receipt shows 11:47pm, and my phone was in my hand when it buzzed.
Exhibit: your message came from the airport wifi login, timestamped 6:12am, so you were on your phone before the flight even boarded.
Exhibit: the kitchen cam from Tuesday shows you grabbing the raw chicken, then the salt shaker, no sink in between.
Exhibit: your apron has raw-chicken smears on the hip where you wiped your hands, and the sink was bone dry.
I am a storm drain; I gulp the standing water down below the street.
I am a pump truck; I suck the remaining water out of the intersection and hose it into the gutter.
I am a bulldozer; I push the fallen rock back out of the lane and clear the tunnel mouth.
I am a rock bolt; I pin the loose tunnel roof so no more rock falls onto the lane.
I am a heavy tow truck; I hook the smoking car and drag it out of the ditch.
I am a fire extinguisher; I spray foam on the smoking car to stop the smoke and fire.
I am a hazmat crew; I soak up the spilled fuel and oil the smoking car left on the road.
I am a traffic signal electrician; I open the box and restore the dark signal's power.
I am a signal control officer; I switch the junction to all-way stop signs and cover the dark signal heads.
I am a traffic officer; I direct every car through the dark junction by hand until the signal is fixed.
I am a fuel truck; I pump gas into the empty tank until it runs.
I am a mechanic; I replace the cracked fuel line so the gas stays in the tank.
I am a drain pan; I catch the leaking gas so the fuel line stops dripping onto the road.
I am a roadside drain; I swallow the muddy water and pull it off the road.
I am a pump truck; I suck the drain clear and haul the muddy water away.
I am a grader; I blade the silted drain channel open so the water drains off the road.
I am a storm drain; I swallow the standing water off the road.
I am a grader; I cut a crown into the asphalt so the water runs off the lane.
I am a shutoff wrench; I crank the hydrant valve closed and stop the water.
I am a sandbag; I stack myself over the broken hydrant and hold the water down.
I am a culvert; I carry the mud off the roadway and under it.
I am a bulldozer; I scrape the mudslide off the asphalt and push it down the embankment.
